newsitem.title: USA: Conoco, PDVSA near finalizing $1.3bn jv financing.
newsitem.headline: Conoco, PDVSA near finalizing $1.3bn jv financing.

text.p: State-owned Petroleos de Venezuela unit Maraven and Dupont energy unit Conoco plan to take a big leap forward Friday on financing their $2.2-billion joint venture to upgrade Venezuelan heavy crude, sources said Thursday.
The companies plan shortly to name two U.S. banks to underwrite the capital markets portion of a $1.3 billion financing package for the joint venture, sources said.
The lead and co-lead banks will be announced tomorrow afternoon after a meeting of the joint venture company, called Petrozuata, they said.
Sources said the financing would be "off balance sheet, non-recourse debt financing" or as close to that as possible.

Petrozuata, a 50-50 joint venture, would produce about 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) of extra-heavy crude from Venezuela's Orinoco Belt, and convert it into about 104,000 bpd of 21-gravity synthetic crude, Conoco officials said.
Drilling will start in 1997 to recover 1.5 billion to 2.0 billion barrels of extra heavy crude.
In 1998, the companies will begin building a delayed coker at the Venezuelan coastal city of Jose to convert the crude. The facility is due on line in 2000.
Petrozuata will first pump 65,000 bpd of extra-heavy oil beginning around August 1998. Another 65,000 bpd will come on stream in late 1999 to coincide with start-up of the coker, Conoco said.
At least part of the syncrude would be processed at Conoco's U.S. refineries, including its Lake Charles facility.
Maraven and Conoco inked their joint venture Nov 10, 1995.

Sources said a number of large banks competed to underwrite the deal, not because the deal itself is particularly profitable but because the winners could get preferential access to more attractive Venezuelan upstream projects in the future.

The Maraven-Conoco venture is the first of five proposed Venezuelan upgrading deals to reach the financing stage, and its success in raising capital would pave the way for the other deals to move forward, sources said.
Other companies involved in separate proposed deals include ARCO, Phillips, Texaco, Mobil and Exxon.
Venezuela's vast Orinoco Tar Belt contains an estimated 270 billion barrels of recoverable crude.
